boxes.label: One of two Options
boxes.bodyHtml: Students choose two of seven HSC Options. World Order is examined purely through extended-response essays in the real HSC exam — there's no official multiple-choice bank for it, so the quiz/trivia questions here test specific facts confirmed in NESA's syllabus and a real trial-exam marking guideline, not invented content.

boxes.label: Aligned to the HSC syllabus
boxes.bodyHtml: Written to the NESA Legal Studies Stage 6 Syllabus, with worked sample answers and named case studies modelled on real HSC exam question styles and marking criteria.

summary.note: Covers all three syllabus sub-topics for this Option, in NESA's own order.

groups.title: The nature of world order
points: World order refers to the system of international relations, rules and institutions that aim to ensure stability, security and cooperation between nation states, both domestically and internationally.

World order has developed significantly over time, particularly through the growth of international law and institutions following the two World Wars — most significantly the creation of the United Nations in 1945, established to maintain peace and security and encourage cooperation between states.

Conflict can be inter-state (between two or more nation states, e.g. Russia's invasion of Ukraine) or intra-state (within a single state, e.g. a civil war), and access to resources (land, water, energy, minerals) is a significant and recurring source of conflict between and within states.

groups.title: Responses to world order
points: The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) is the UN's main body responsible for maintaining international peace and security. It has 15 members: the five permanent members (the P5 — the US, UK, France, Russia and China) and 10 other members elected for two-year terms. Under Article 27(3) of the UN Charter, any one of the P5 can veto a resolution, meaning the UNSC can only act with the agreement of all five permanent members.

Legal responses include treaties and international law, courts and tribunals (e.g. the International Court of Justice, which resolves disputes between states, and the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals), UN-authorised sanctions (e.g. UNSC Resolution 2270, which imposed cargo inspections and banking restrictions on North Korea in response to its weapons program) and UN peacekeeping missions — authorised either under Chapter VI of the UN Charter (peaceful settlement of disputes, with the consent of the parties) or the more forceful Chapter VII (authorising the use of force), as seen in missions to East Timor and the Central African Republic.

Key international instruments for regulating the conduct of hostilities include the Geneva Conventions (1949) and their Additional Protocols (1977 and 2005), which set out the international humanitarian law rules of armed conflict, alongside weapons-control treaties such as the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, the Convention on Cluster Munitions, the Biological Weapons Convention and the Chemical Weapons Convention.

Non-legal responses include diplomacy and political negotiation between states, the use (or threatened use) of force outside a UN mandate, media coverage that raises international awareness of a conflict, and advocacy by non-government organisations and intergovernmental organisations — none of which carry the same binding legal force as a UN Security Council resolution, but which can still influence state behaviour.

groups.title: Contemporary issues concerning world order
points: The principle of 'responsibility to protect' (R2P), adopted at the 2005 UN World Summit, holds that the international community has a responsibility to intervene when a state manifestly fails to protect its own population, built on three pillars: protecting (a state's own primary responsibility to protect its population), intervening (the international community's responsibility to intervene if a state fails to do so) and rebuilding (assisting recovery after intervention). R2P is not itself binding international law, and has been invoked in practice only rarely — most notably when the UNSC authorised military intervention in Libya in 2011 under Resolution 1973. While this quickly removed the Gaddafi government, the international community largely failed to fulfil the third pillar (rebuilding), and Libya descended into further civil war in 2013 and continued instability contributing to the broader European migration crisis.

Regional and global situations that continue to threaten peace and security include the Russia-Ukraine conflict (an inter-state war where Russia, as a P5 member, has repeatedly used its Security Council veto to block resolutions condemning its own actions, including blocking a referral of the conflict to the International Criminal Court), the Syrian civil war (where Russia and China have used their vetoes more than a dozen times to block humanitarian and military action, including blocking the referral of former president Bashar al-Assad to the ICC for alleged war crimes), and territorial disputes in the South China Sea, which have largely been addressed through diplomatic negotiation rather than binding legal resolution.

The success of global cooperation in achieving world order is mixed: UNSC Resolution 2270's sanctions regime against North Korea show that binding, unanimous Security Council action is possible and can meaningfully restrict a state's conduct, but the repeated use of the P5 veto during the Syrian civil war shows that the same institution can also be rendered powerless whenever a permanent member's own interests are at stake.

Rules regarding the conduct of hostilities, set out in the Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law more broadly, aim to limit the humanitarian cost of armed conflict (e.g. protecting civilians and prisoners of war) — but their effectiveness depends heavily on voluntary compliance by parties to a conflict, since there is no single global police force able to enforce them directly on a battlefield.

questions.questionHtml: How successful have legal and non-legal mechanisms been in maintaining world order? Support your response with at least ONE contemporary issue.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Cover both legal responses (UN Charter, courts, tribunals, treaties) and non-legal responses (diplomacy, media, NGOs) separately.
  • Integrate at least one contemporary issue explicitly.
  • Reach a clear, supported judgement on effectiveness.
Sample answer

Legal and non-legal mechanisms have had mixed success in maintaining world order, with outcomes heavily shaped by state sovereignty and the interests of the most powerful states. The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) is the main judicial/political organ tasked with maintaining peace, and can act decisively when its five permanent members agree — as shown by UNSC Resolution 2270, which imposed detailed cargo-inspection and banking sanctions on North Korea, demonstrating the effectiveness of binding legal cooperation when achieved.

However, the UNSC's veto power under Article 27(3) of the UN Charter allows any one of the five permanent members to block a resolution, regardless of the other 14 members' views. This has severely limited legal responses to the Syrian civil war, where Russia and China have repeatedly vetoed resolutions authorising humanitarian or military action, including blocking a referral of the conflict to the International Criminal Court, showing that the same law that enables cooperation can also entrench inaction whenever it conflicts with a permanent member's own interests.

Non-legal responses — diplomatic negotiation, media coverage, and advocacy by non-government organisations — have complemented legal responses by raising international awareness and applying political pressure, but cannot compel state compliance the way a binding UNSC resolution can. Overall, legal and non-legal mechanisms have succeeded in maintaining world order in some instances, but remain ultimately limited by the extent to which the most powerful states are themselves willing to comply with, or permit, international action.

questions.questionHtml: "International institutions built in 1945 cannot keep pace with a world that has moved on." Assess this claim in the context of how nation states pursue peace and resolve conflict with one another.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain 'law lag' directly in relation to world order.
  • Balance an example of adaptation with an example of lagging behind.
  • Reach an explicit judgement.
Sample answer

This claim holds up to a considerable extent when it comes to maintaining world order. The principle of 'responsibility to protect' (R2P), adopted at the 2005 UN World Summit, represented an attempt to modernise the international community's response to states failing to protect their own populations — but R2P is not binding international law, and has been invoked meaningfully only once, in Libya in 2011 under UNSC Resolution 1973. Even then, the international community fulfilled only the 'intervening' pillar of R2P and largely failed the 'rebuilding' pillar, leaving Libya in continued instability. This shows the law adapting in principle faster than institutions can actually implement it in practice.

The persistent use of the P5 veto power under Article 27(3) of the UN Charter is a clearer example of legal rigidity failing to keep pace with global community expectations: despite the scale of civilian harm in the Syrian civil war, Russia and China's vetoes have repeatedly prevented the UN Security Council from taking binding action, including blocking accountability mechanisms like referral to the International Criminal Court. The composition and veto structure of the Security Council has remained essentially unchanged since 1945, even as the geopolitical balance of power and international expectations around civilian protection have shifted substantially.

On the other hand, some legal mechanisms have adapted meaningfully: the growth of ad hoc and permanent international tribunals since the 1990s (from the ICTY and ICTR to a permanent International Criminal Court) reflects a real, if slow, institutionalisation of the international community's response to mass atrocities. Overall, while some aspects of international law relating to world order have evolved, its most powerful institution — the Security Council — remains structurally almost identical to its 1945 design, supporting the view that the international system built after WWII has struggled to keep pace with the world it now governs.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the three pillars of the 'responsibility to protect' (R2P) principle and assess how effectively they were applied in Libya in 2011.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name and explain all three pillars.
  • Apply them specifically to the 2011 Libyan intervention.
  • Reach a judgement on effectiveness.
Sample answer

R2P, adopted at the 2005 World Summit, is based on three pillars: protecting (a state's own primary responsibility to protect its population), intervening (the international community's responsibility to intervene if a state manifestly fails to do so) and rebuilding (assisting recovery once intervention has occurred). In 2011, the UN Security Council authorised military intervention in Libya under Resolution 1973, marking the first time R2P's second pillar was used in this way, and a NATO-led force helped depose the Gaddafi government relatively quickly.

However, the international community did not effectively fulfil the third pillar. Libya descended into a further civil war by 2013 and continued to experience instability that has contributed to broader regional issues, including migration pressures into Europe. This shows R2P's protecting and intervening pillars can be applied relatively effectively when the Security Council agrees to act, but the rebuilding pillar — arguably the hardest to achieve — has, in Libya's case, been largely unfulfilled, limiting the overall effectiveness of R2P as a complete framework for achieving world order.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the difference between a Chapter VI and a Chapter VII UN peacekeeping mission.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain Chapter VI.
  • Explain Chapter VII.
  • State the key difference.
Sample answer

A Chapter VI mission (the 'pacific settlement of disputes' provisions of the UN Charter) involves the UN facilitating negotiation and mediation, and deploying peacekeepers only with the consent of the parties involved — typically to monitor an already-agreed ceasefire or peace agreement.

A Chapter VII mission allows the Security Council to authorise more forceful measures, including the use of military force, where it finds a genuine threat to international peace and security exists — without needing the consent of all parties, as seen in UN-authorised missions to East Timor and the Central African Republic. The key difference is therefore consent: Chapter VI missions operate with it, while Chapter VII missions can be authorised without it.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the significance of the International Criminal Court (ICC) to world order.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State when/how the ICC was established.
  • Explain its significance compared to earlier tribunals.
  • Note a real limitation.
Sample answer

The International Criminal Court (ICC) was established under the Rome Statute, adopted in 1998 and entering into force in 2002, as the first permanent international court able to prosecute individuals — not just states — for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and the crime of aggression.

Its significance lies in the shift from earlier ad hoc tribunals, such as the ICTY and ICTR (each created individually, after the fact, to address one specific conflict), to a standing institution intended to deter future atrocities through the ongoing possibility of individual criminal accountability. However, the ICC relies entirely on state cooperation to make arrests, since it has no independent police force, and several major powers — including the United States, Russia and China — are not parties to the Rome Statute, significantly limiting its practical jurisdiction and enforcement power.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the effectiveness of the United Nations Security Council veto power in achieving world order.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain Article 27(3) and the P5 veto.
  • Give a strength and a real limitation, with examples.
  • Reach a judgement.
Sample answer

Under Article 27(3) of the UN Charter, any one of the Security Council's five permanent members (the P5 — the US, UK, France, Russia and China) can veto a resolution, meaning the Council can only take binding action with the agreement of all five. Requiring this unanimity was originally intended to keep the major powers engaged within the UN system after 1945, rather than acting entirely outside it, and can encourage negotiation and compromise before a resolution is put to a vote.

In practice, however, the veto frequently paralyses the Council whenever a permanent member's own interests, or those of its allies, are implicated — Russia and China have used their vetoes more than a dozen times to block humanitarian and accountability measures relating to the Syrian civil war, including blocking a referral of the conflict to the International Criminal Court, and Russia has also used its veto in relation to resolutions concerning its own invasion of Ukraine. Overall, the veto power is a double-edged mechanism: it was designed to keep the world's most powerful states bound into a rules-based system, but its modern effect is often to prevent that same system from acting against a P5 member or its allies.

questions.questionHtml: Outline the purpose of the Geneva Conventions (1949).
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State what they regulate.
  • State who they protect.
Sample answer

The Geneva Conventions (1949), together with their Additional Protocols (1977 and 2005), set out the core rules of international humanitarian law — the law regulating the conduct of armed conflict. Their purpose is to protect people who are not, or are no longer, taking part in hostilities, including wounded and sick soldiers, shipwrecked military personnel, prisoners of war, and civilians — setting minimum standards of treatment that are meant to apply regardless of which side is winning or considered to be in the right.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how weapons-control treaties contribute to world order.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name at least two real weapons-control treaties.
  • Explain how they contribute to world order.
  • Note their limitation.
Sample answer

Weapons-control treaties — including the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, the Convention on Cluster Munitions, the Biological Weapons Convention and the Chemical Weapons Convention — aim to reduce the risk and scale of future conflict by limiting the development, possession or use of the most destructive categories of weapons, and often create monitoring or inspection regimes that help build trust between states.

However, like other international treaties, they rely on voluntary ratification and ongoing compliance: a state that chooses not to ratify a treaty (or later withdraws from it) is not bound by it, and detecting covert non-compliance — such as a hidden weapons program — remains genuinely difficult, limiting how confidently these treaties can be enforced in practice.

questions.questionHtml: Discuss the effectiveness of 'responsibility to protect' (R2P) as a response to threats to world order.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain R2P and its legal status.
  • Discuss its one clear real-world application.
  • Note how rarely it has actually been used, and why.
Sample answer

'Responsibility to protect' (R2P), adopted at the 2005 UN World Summit, holds that the international community has a responsibility to intervene when a state manifestly fails to protect its own population, built on three pillars: protecting, intervening and rebuilding. R2P is not itself binding international law — it is a political and moral principle that still depends on the Security Council agreeing to act in any given case.

R2P has been invoked to authorise military intervention only once, in Libya in 2011 under Resolution 1973: the 'intervening' pillar succeeded in helping remove the Gaddafi government relatively quickly, but the international community failed to fulfil the 'rebuilding' pillar, and Libya descended into further civil war by 2013. Since then, R2P has not been used to authorise intervention in other serious situations, including the Syrian civil war, largely because Russia and China's Security Council vetoes have blocked any such resolution — showing R2P's practical application depends entirely on the same P5 veto politics that limit other UN action, rather than operating as an automatic, independent legal trigger. Overall, R2P represented a significant normative development in world order, but has proven effective only on the rare occasion that P5 interests happen to align, giving it limited real-world reach so far.

trivia.answerHtml: The system of international relations, rules and institutions that aim to ensure stability, security and cooperation between nation states.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between inter-state and intra-state conflict?
trivia.answerHtml: Inter-state conflict is between two or more nation states; intra-state conflict is within a single state (e.g. a civil war).

trivia.questionHtml: How many members does the UN Security Council have, and how are they split?
trivia.answerHtml: 15 members — 5 permanent members (the P5) and 10 elected members serving two-year terms.

trivia.questionHtml: Who are the five permanent members (P5) of the UN Security Council?
trivia.answerHtml: The United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia and China.

trivia.questionHtml: What power does Article 27(3) of the UN Charter give each P5 member?
trivia.answerHtml: The power to veto (block) any UN Security Council resolution.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between a Chapter VI and a Chapter VII UN peacekeeping mission?
trivia.answerHtml: Chapter VI missions involve peaceful settlement with the parties' consent; Chapter VII missions can authorise the use of force.

trivia.questionHtml: Name two international courts relevant to world order and what each does.
trivia.answerHtml: The International Court of Justice resolves disputes between states; the International Criminal Court prosecutes individuals for the most serious crimes.
Imposed cargo-inspection and banking-restriction sanctions on North Korea in response to its weapons program.

trivia.questionHtml: What do the Geneva Conventions (1949) regulate?
trivia.answerHtml: International humanitarian law — the rules for the conduct of armed conflict, including protection of civilians and prisoners of war.

trivia.questionHtml: Name two weapons-control treaties relevant to world order.
trivia.answerHtml: Any two of: the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, the Convention on Cluster Munitions, the Biological Weapons Convention, or the Chemical Weapons Convention.

trivia.questionHtml: What are the three pillars of the 'responsibility to protect' (R2P) principle?
When was R2P adopted, and is it binding international law?
trivia.answerHtml: Adopted at the 2005 UN World Summit — it is not itself binding international law.

trivia.questionHtml: When was R2P first used to authorise military intervention, and where?
trivia.answerHtml: 2011, in Libya, under UN Security Council Resolution 1973.

trivia.questionHtml: What happened after the 2011 Libyan intervention that shows a limitation of R2P?
trivia.answerHtml: The international community largely failed R2P's 'rebuilding' pillar — Libya descended into further civil war in 2013 and continued instability.

trivia.questionHtml: How has Russia used its Security Council veto in relation to the Syrian civil war?
trivia.answerHtml: To repeatedly block resolutions authorising humanitarian or military action, including blocking a referral of the conflict to the International Criminal Court.

trivia.questionHtml: How has the South China Sea territorial dispute mainly been addressed?
trivia.answerHtml: Largely through diplomatic negotiation rather than binding legal resolution.

trivia.questionHtml: Give an example of a non-legal response to a world order issue.
trivia.answerHtml: Diplomacy/political negotiation between states, or media coverage/NGO advocacy raising international awareness.

trivia.questionHtml: When was the United Nations established, and why?
trivia.answerHtml: 1945, to maintain international peace and security and encourage cooperation between states after the World Wars.
